overview: This strictly confidential file concerns the refusal of the Japanese shipping company Osaka Syosen Kaisya—acting through the captain of the M.S. “Brazil Maru”—to carry Paul Mutter and W. Leverman from Buenos Aires despite their valid passports, visas, and prepaid first-class fares. The company reported that Mr. and Mrs. Jaeger, previously rejected from other sailings, had been accepted, leaving Mutter and Leverman as the only passengers still excluded. The correspondence notes uncertainty about Japanese policy toward nationals of belligerent countries and observes that Japanese authorities were nevertheless issuing visas to men of military age. The bundle consists of a confidential filing sheet, a State Department air-mail instruction to the American Embassy in Buenos Aires, and the underlying February 3, 1941 government-agency letter circulated to State, naval intelligence, and military intelligence officials.

subfiles.title: Confidential filing sheet for decimal file 894.856/1
subfiles.about: A filing marker identifies the material as confidential and assigns it decimal number 894.856/1.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains only the file number 894.856/1 and the notation that the material was filed confidentially. It serves as the archival cover or filing marker for the substantive correspondence that follows.

subfiles.title: Air-mail instruction No. 671 on passengers refused by the Brazil Maru
subfiles.about: The Secretary of State confidentially relays intelligence about the Brazil Maru captain’s refusal to carry Paul Mutter and W. Leverman.
subfiles.summary: The instruction quotes a February 3 letter from an official U.S. agency reporting that Osaka Syosen Kaisya’s New York office had informed its Buenos Aires office that the captain of the M.S. “Brazil Maru” refused passage to Paul Mutter and W. Leverman without a specific explanation beyond the international situation. Both men possessed passports and visas and had each paid $300 in New York for first-class passage. Mr. and Mrs. Jaeger were accepted despite earlier refusals, leaving Mutter and Leverman as the only rejected passengers; the company had received no written change in Japanese policy toward belligerent nationals, while Japanese authorities continued granting visas even to military-age men.

subfiles.title: Government-agency letter to Berle concerning Brazil Maru passengers
subfiles.about: The source letter reports confidential information about Japanese acceptance and rejection of passengers and distributes it to State, naval, and military intelligence officials.
subfiles.summary: The first page is largely represented in the OCR by confidential handling and filing stamps, while the surviving second page concludes the discussion of Japanese treatment of passengers from belligerent countries. It states that no written policy change had been received from Japanese authorities but that visas were apparently being granted even to military-age passengers. The letter is signed in OCR as “J. R. Howler,” evidently a misreading of J. Edgar Hoover, and copies were sent to Captain Jules James of Naval Intelligence and Brigadier General Sherman Miles of Army G-2.

interest: The file provides a compact case study of how commercial passenger decisions by a Japanese steamship line were monitored as intelligence during the tense months before the United States entered the Pacific War. Particularly useful is the contrast between valid travel documentation and the ship captain’s unexplained discretionary refusal, as well as the unequal treatment of passengers who had apparently faced earlier rejections. The circulation of the underlying report among Berle, Naval Intelligence, and Army G-2 shows how an ostensibly minor shipping dispute entered interdepartmental security channels, while the quoted material preserves details about fares, offices, and visa practices that may assist research into wartime mobility and surveillance.
